exclusions.no_leave_one_out_baseline: {count} queries make up so much of their own band that removing them leaves nothing to compare against.

quickWins.limitationsTitle: What this will not tell you

limitations.serp_cause_unobserved: Why the CTR is low. A gap can mean your title is weak, or that searchers wanted something else, or that Google answered the query in the results page so nobody needed to click. We do not detect SERP features and those are a leading cause of exactly these gaps. Read a few of the actual queries before rewriting anything.
limitations.site_level_low_ctr_band: One or more position bands on your site earn under 1% overall. Every query in such a band sits below baseline for the same structural reason, so they are one fact rather than a dozen.
limitations.insufficient_bucket_sample: No position band had enough impressions and distinct queries to serve as a baseline. We would rather say we could not look than compute a number from four queries.
limitations.insufficient_query_sample: Your bands are measurable, but no single query cleared the 100-impression floor. That is a statement about sample size, not about your site.
limitations.high_query_anonymization_gap: A large share of your impressions and clicks never appear in Search Console’s query report. Everything here is computed on what Google returns, which is not everything.
limitations.partial_gsc_export: Search Console had more rows than we read. Rows come back ordered by clicks descending, so what got cut is the low-click end — which is exactly the part this table looks for.
limitations.brand_segment_insufficient_evidence: We excluded your brand queries from the baseline, but there are too few of them to say anything about the brand segment separately.
limitations.aggregation_basis_mismatch: The property total and the query rows were not measured on the same basis, so we cannot compute how much Search Console withheld. Search Console picks its own aggregation once a query groups or filters by page, and dividing one basis by another produces a number that describes neither.
limitations.anonymization_gap_uncomputable: We could not size what Search Console withheld: either the property reported no totals for this window, or the query rows added up to more than the property total. The two readings disagree, so we are not reporting a share rather than reporting a wrong one.

quickWins.emptyBody: That is not the same as “no opportunities”. See what we could not measure, below.
quickWins.storageNote: We do not store your results. Export or note anything you want to keep before you close the tab. We deliberately do not offer a before/after comparison: a re-run weeks later cannot separate the effect of an edit from seasonal demand, and presenting it as if it could would be the one claim this tool exists to avoid.

quickWins.actionsIntro: Every line here is gated on a number in this same report, and names the rows it came from. None of it predicts what a change would do — this tool does not model that, and the places where you would most want it to are exactly the places it says so.

apply_wording_candidates.title: Compare each candidate against the page it copies
apply_wording_candidates.body: For {candidateCount} of your queries we found a page on your own site, in the same position band, earning clearly more. The drafts further down rewrite the title and description in that page’s pattern. Open both before you apply anything: you are copying a pattern that demonstrably works on your site, which beats any template — but it is still a pattern, not an explanation of the gap.

open_serps_for_top_gaps.title: Search these yourself and look at what sits above you
open_serps_for_top_gaps.body: {serpRowCount} rows fall short of your own curve by more than a single click and have no comparable page on your site to learn from. The missing piece is the results page itself: an AI Overview, a featured snippet, a video carousel or a People-Also-Ask block takes the click before your listing is read, and we observe none of them. Search each query in a private window and note what sits above position 1. If the page is plain and your listing is still skipped, then the title and description are the candidate. The largest shortfall here is {largestGapClicks} clicks.

size_the_withheld_share.title: Find out how much never reached this table
size_the_withheld_share.body: Search Console withholds queries below an undisclosed volume threshold — here that is {withheldImpressionShare} of impressions and {withheldClickShare} of clicks, where a dash means we could not size it, which is never the same as zero. Open the Performance report and compare its own totals against the query tab. The difference is the part no query-level tool can see, and on a small site most of the demand lives there.

check_pages_report.title: Switch to the Pages report — most of your queries are too small to appear here
check_pages_report.body: {belowFloorCount} queries had fewer than 100 impressions in this window, against {measuredRowCount} that cleared the floor. One click either way would change their rate completely, so we leave them out rather than publish a rate we do not believe. Search Console’s Pages tab aggregates them: a pattern that is invisible query by query is often plain page by page.

read_low_band_as_one_finding.title: Don’t rewrite a low band one query at a time
read_low_band_as_one_finding.body: Positions {bands} earn under 1% overall on your site, and {lowBandRowCount} of the rows above sit there. Every one of them is below baseline for the same structural reason, so they are one fact rather than {lowBandRowCount}. Published tables predict 3–7% at these positions; we tested that against a real site and measured a tenth of it. Whatever is happening applies to the band — start there, not with the individual titles.

avoid_curve_as_law.title: Your curve does not fall the way rank tables say it should
avoid_curve_as_law.body: Positions {firstBand} earn {higherBandCtr} on your site, while {secondBand} — ranking lower — earn {lowerBandCtr}. That is not a measurement error, it is what your queries do: what people search for changes with the position you hold, and a lower band full of specific, high-intent queries can out-earn a higher band full of vague ones. It also means the baseline inside the higher band is weak evidence about any single row in it.

avoid_gap_as_forecast.title: The gap column adds up to {totalGapClicks} clicks. Rewriting will not hand them to you.
avoid_gap_as_forecast.body: The gap is expected clicks minus observed clicks, where expected comes from your own site’s rate at that position. Both sides are measured and so is the difference. It is not a forecast: nothing here models the effect of a change, and the leading cause of gaps like these is a results page that answered the query so nobody needed to click. Read {totalGapClicks} as the size of the question, not the size of the prize.

compare_with_own_page.label: Has a control
compare_with_own_page.hint: A page on your own site, in the same position band, earns clearly more. That page is the comparison — there is a draft below modelled on it.

read_the_serp.label: Check the SERP
read_the_serp.hint: Short by more than a click, with no comparable page on your site. The missing information is on the results page, which you can see and we cannot.

band_is_the_story.label: Band-wide
band_is_the_story.hint: The whole position band earns under 1%. These rows are below baseline for one shared reason, so rewriting them one at a time treats one fact as many.

gap_within_noise.label: Under one click
gap_within_noise.hint: The shortfall is smaller than a single click. Clicks are counted in whole numbers, so prediction and observation agree as closely as the unit allows.

at_or_above_curve.label: At or above
at_or_above_curve.hint: At or better than what your site earns at this position. Kept in the table as context, not as work.

keywordMap.emptyBodyPartial: Part of this run did not complete, so some candidates were never judged at all rather than judged and dropped. The counts above show which gates actually ran; until the missing stage recovers, an empty list here is not evidence that there is nothing to find.
keywordMap.clustersTitle: Lexically related terms — review before merging
keywordMap.clustersIntro: Terms whose wording overlaps enough that one page could serve them all. Only groups of two or more are listed. Grouping is lexical and does not prove page-one overlap, so this is a review suggestion, not a site structure.
keywordMap.weakestHint: Weakest rank is one raw page-one fact, not the decision rule by itself. The opportunity decision uses three separately reported signals: a young domain, a low-organic-traffic domain, or a community result. A positive signal still qualifies the row; only a row with no positive signal falls back to incomplete-on-unavailable evidence.
keywordMap.geoHint: These are question-form candidates judged by the same three page-one signals. A related or source page is shown with its exact basis; no demand is claimed when the provider returned none.
keywordMap.eligibleIntro: At least one required opportunity signal was observed. AI Overview answer completeness can lower ordering; it never excludes a candidate.
keywordMap.withheldIntro: These candidates received an exclusion decision. Each exact reason is preserved instead of being folded into missing evidence.
keywordMap.incompleteIntro: These candidates were attempted, but a required evidence source did not complete. They were not rejected; the missing evidence is named below.
keywordMap.incompleteRetry: Retry the unchanged run after the missing evidence source recovers. A retry before recovery is likely to reproduce the same gap.
keywordMap.withheldGuidance: An explicit provider zero is a completed snapshot. A three-signal negative may change as the results page changes; review it later rather than treating it as missing evidence.

faq.title: What this does and does not tell you

items.q: Where does the score come from?
items.a: Each check on this page is worth a set number of points; the score is their sum, restated out of 100. The weights are ours, not Google's — the number measures how well this page does the part it controls, not whether it will rank. A few conditions hold the score down on their own: a page that declares noindex, returns an error status, carries almost no copy, or is not about the keyword you gave. In those cases no amount of other work reaches a search result.

items.q: Why does the first check take minutes?
items.a: Your page is read out of a site-wide collection rather than fetched on its own. A second check on the same site within the hour reuses that collection and returns in seconds; after that the collection has expired and the crawl runs again.

items.q: Will a high count rank the page?
items.a: No. Where a keyword sits on a page is one input among site authority, page experience, competition and behaviour. This measures the input it can actually see.

items.q: How many queries can I check at once, and how do I type them?
items.a: Up to five, all in the one field, separated by commas — both the ASCII comma and the full-width one, and a newline counts too. Repeats are folded into one, anything past five is not submitted, and the field says how many it dropped. One query is marked primary: most fields covered wins, then the longer query, then the order you typed them. Topic focus in the score reads that one query only, so adding exploratory words alongside your real target cannot lower the page's score.

items.q: Are brand terms treated differently?
items.a: They are labelled, and that is all — no points either way. The test is mechanical: the hostname is split into labels and compared against what you typed. The result is published as an observation, never as score, because a brand term sits at a density that would read as thin for a topic term and judging the same number twice is not honest. A single CJK word has no Latin label to compare against, so it is marked not applicable rather than not matched.

items.q: Why is keyword density not scored?
items.a: Because two different denominators appear on this page and mixing them produces opposite conclusions. The per-query density is measured inside the captured text — title, description, the heading set and the opening passage — where a normally optimised page already sits near 20%, so the familiar 0.5%–3% band would call a well-built page keyword stuffing. The whole-page term tables use the page body's counting units instead. Both numbers name their own denominator, but they cannot be compared, so we report them and grade neither.

items.q: How do I read the whole-page term tables?
items.a: The page body is cut into one- to five-word combinations, with the top 15 kept for each length. Term density is occurrences divided by total units. Occupancy density is occurrences times phrase length divided by total units, so phrases of different lengths can be compared — overlapping occurrences are counted each time, which is why a long phrase on a page that repeats one word can exceed 100%. Function words are removed from the single-word table only; phrase tables keep them, because "the astrology of" is how people actually write.

items.q: Why is JavaScript not executed?
items.a: The crawl reads the HTML the server returned, so body copy, components and links mounted by front-end script are invisible to this tool. It does not pretend otherwise: one check reports whether the body text is in the static HTML at all. When it is not, the word count and the coverage on this page were both measured under that condition — do not read them as what a browser finishes rendering.

items.q: Where does the search-results section get its data?
items.a: From a third-party search-results source, for the market and language you picked above, as one desktop sample of page one: who holds the top positions, whether you are among them, and how many carry sitelinks. Results move daily, so this is a snapshot rather than a ranking history or a difficulty score. It is also the one paid call this tool makes, which is why market and language are lists — an unsupported pair never leaves a request at all.

items.q: Does it work on Chinese pages?
items.a: Yes. Body length counts one unit per CJK character. Title and description length is measured in display width, with CJK characters counted as two, which lands closer to where a search result actually truncates. The term tables split on the same basis.

items.q: Where are my past checks stored?
items.a: In this browser only. It is not an account archive: clearing storage, switching browsers or signing out loses it. When one page has been checked more than once, the list shows how its score and coverage moved.

items.q: How is this different from the SEO Agent?
items.a: They run the same site-wide crawl. This tool reads the one page you named out of that crawl and answers around the queries you gave; the Agent reads the whole site. That is why the first check waits for the crawl, and why the same site checked again within the hour comes back in seconds. The report hands this page and its queries straight to the Agent.

items.q: Does it cost credits?
items.a: No. The tool is free while it is being tested.

fixes.title: What to change on this page
fixes.homepage: A homepage is judged on whether the primary term is unmistakable: put it in the title, the H1 and the first sentence of the body, and let the sub-headings carry the secondary terms rather than repeating the primary one.
fixes.product: A product page competes on specificity. Keep the product's own name in the title and H1, and let the target term appear where it describes what the product does, not as a phrase bolted onto the front of the name.
fixes.tool: A tool page is found by what it does. The title and H1 should read as the job the visitor came to do, and the opening text should say the tool runs here rather than describing it from the outside.
fixes.guide: A guide is found by the question it answers. Put the question's own words in the title and H1, and use the sub-headings for the sub-questions so a reader scanning them can see the answer is here.
fixes.basis: Guidance for the page role you declared. It does not change any count above, and none of it is a claim about ranking.

coverage.title: What this checks, and what it does not
coverage.intro: What follows is everything it can actually read. Anything not listed gets no verdict — stating the edge here beats leaving you to infer it from a report that never mentions it.

checks.meta: Title, description, canonical, robots directives, viewport, encoding, language, favicon. Lengths are measured by display width, with CJK characters counting double.
checks.content: Body length (characters for CJK), H1 count and length, H2–H6 sub-heading count, text-to-markup ratio, and whether the page carries anything a visitor can act through.
checks.keyword: Where your submitted queries land in the title, description, H1, sub-headings, opening text and URL, plus a whole-page leaderboard of one- to five-word phrases.
checks.links: Internal outlinks, empty anchor text, external destinations and their rel safety.
checks.media: Image alt coverage, declared width and height, and lazy loading.
checks.social: Open Graph title/description/image, Twitter card, and JSON-LD types and parse errors.
checks.technical: HTTPS, status and redirects, response time, URL shape, HTML weight, hreflang, robots.txt and sitemap reachability, sitemap membership, and whether the body is in the static HTML.
checks.site: The ones only a full-site crawl can answer: duplicate titles and descriptions, sitemap pages nothing links to, broken outbound links, and click depth.
checks.serp: Page one for your primary query in the market you chose: who holds the top ten, whether you are among them, and how many results show sitelinks.

not.rendering: It does not run JavaScript. Content, components and links mounted by client script are invisible to it — it will tell you whether the body is in the static HTML, but not what the page looks like after the script runs.
not.css: It does not read stylesheets. Text hidden with CSS and boxes reserved with aspect-ratio are both outside what it can judge.
not.ranking: It does not predict rankings or score difficulty. The results-page section is one sample taken now, not a trend.
not.backlinks: It does not look at backlinks, domain authority or traffic. What this page cannot change about itself is outside its scope.
not.headings: It does not give a heading outline. The crawl does not retain H2–H6 levels, so sub-headings can only be one merged list.
not.density: It does not grade keyword density. The denominator is the captured text, where a correctly optimised page already reads around 20% — a band borrowed from whole-body density would call that page stuffed.

pageCitability.limitsTitle: What this check does not do

limits.noJavaScript: It does not run JavaScript. A page whose copy only appears after hydration is reported as HTML without copy, because that is what a crawler that does not render sees.
limits.boundedRendering: Two fresh Chromium contexts compare the same HTML with JavaScript off and on, within 12 seconds, 40 GET requests and 2 MB. Public images/media/fonts are intentionally omitted; private targets, workers, sockets, downloads and navigation are blocked. Original HTTP CSP is not preserved; a stricter safety policy is applied. This measures controlled body text, not full image/layout fidelity or every browser. Incomplete captures have no ratio.
limits.onePage: It reads one page plus that host's robots.txt and llms.txt. It does not crawl the site and does not fetch the canonical target.
limits.noRanking: It says nothing about ranking, traffic or whether any model has actually cited the page. It describes the page, not the market.
limits.advisoryRows: ClaudeBot and GPTBot training access, Google-Extended Gemini training/grounding controls and /llms.txt are outside the generic pass count. Claude-SearchBot search and Claude-User user-directed fetching are not measured. Google Search crawling, AI Overviews and AI Mode use separate Search controls.
limits.heuristicRows: Three rows use pattern matching, not semantic or factual verification: opening-answer markers, quantified conditions, and numeric source cues. Review their evidence before acting.
limits.truncation: It reads a bounded slice of the page. When a document exceeds it, every check that would report an absence says it could not read instead.

items.q: Does passing every row mean a model will cite the page?
items.a: No. These rows describe access and shape: whether a crawler is allowed in, whether the copy is in the HTML, and whether a claim can be lifted out. Whether any model actually answers with your page depends on the question asked and on what else exists on the web. This tool never claims otherwise.

items.q: Why are ClaudeBot and GPTBot shown but not counted?
items.a: ClaudeBot and GPTBot collect training material. Blocking them does not establish a retrieval failure. Anthropic uses Claude-SearchBot for search and Claude-User for user-directed fetching; neither is measured here. Google-Extended additionally controls Gemini grounding in Gemini Apps and Vertex AI, not Google Search inclusion or ranking, including AI Overviews and AI Mode. These controls remain separate from a generic citation score.

items.q: Why does a missing robots.txt pass?
items.a: RFC 9309 treats an unavailable robots.txt as full allowance, so a site with no file is not blocking anyone. An unreachable robots.txt, such as a 500, is different: the site's rules are unknown, and that row says so rather than guessing.

items.q: The page looks fine in my browser but the HTML row failed.
items.a: The check compares the exact fetched HTML with an isolated Chromium render. If most copy appears only after scripts execute, a non-rendering reader receives less content. The report shows both captures; blocked resources, truncation or a missing renderer make the comparison unknown instead of passing it.

items.q: Why does freezing matter?
items.a: A visibility run points at a frozen version. If the knowledge base could change underneath it, two runs would not be comparable, and the report could not say which names it was matching on. Freezing is what makes "the same question set, asked again" a true sentence.

items.q: How are generated questions different from calibrated retrieval probes?
items.a: Semantic questions use your reviewed roles, pain points, criteria and source evidence, and you inspect them before freezing. They are uncalibrated and do not enter calibrated citation metrics. Measured retrieval probes remain a separate, clearly identified cohort. Freezing saves the exact reviewed question set rather than generating it again.

items.q: Why must a competitor's name be confirmed separately from its domain?
items.a: A model writes "Linear", not "linear.app". Counting a mention needs the name; knowing where a citation points needs the domain. An unconfirmed competitor stays in the list and out of the share figures, and the report names it as excluded.

items.q: Where do the subtopics come from?
items.a: An owned visibility run supplies the actual headings and list lead-ins from its successful answers. Their cross-sample counts exclude failed calls. Without a run, the brief contains only frozen requirements and facts, or your explicitly labelled manual question; it does not invent observations or buy a replacement sample.

items.q: Can it write the numbers for me?
items.a: No, and that is deliberate. Anything specific comes from the fact table you verified in your knowledge base. A dimension you have not verified is printed as not verified, with the reason. The model that assembles the brief is told it may never state a fact that is not in that table.

items.q: Why is a sampled answer not a source of facts?
items.a: Because it is another company's model, answering once, and it can be wrong. It is good evidence about what a page has to cover — that is what it is used for — and no evidence at all about what is true of your product.

items.q: Does it write the page?
items.a: The Brief does not write or publish the page. It hands the same versioned contract to the shared Content Draft tool, whose sentences are constrained by the non-null fact table. After you publish, the GEO draft links to the page citability check.

aiVisibility.limitsTitle: What this run does not tell you

limits.oneSurface: One surface: ChatGPT answers collected through the DataForSEO API. Not a consumer session, and not Google, Perplexity, Claude or Gemini.
limits.notAttribution: Observed gaps are not causal explanations of a model's answer or proof of future growth. Any site inventory is bounded and explicitly scoped; incomplete page evidence cannot establish absence.
limits.sampledNotCensus: It is a sample. The same question can cite four sources one minute and none the next, which is why each is asked several times and why every number carries its interval.
limits.demandQuestions: Questions written the way a buyer would ask usually get answered from memory. Their mentions are worth counting; their citations are reported without a denominator.
limits.englishOnly: The questions are in English, because that is the language the wording was measured in. A market other than the calibrated one is reported as such.
limits.notStored: This run was not saved. The report is complete, but it could not be written to the store, so it will not be the baseline your next run is compared against.
limits.denseScriptMatching: In a script written without spaces — Chinese, Japanese, Thai — the matcher has no word boundary to hold it to. It finds the brand name inside a longer word as readily as on its own, so a longer word that contains the name counts as a mention here and the count may be higher than the answers warrant.
limits.confirmedSubset: Share of voice covers only the site and confirmed competitor brands, not the whole market.
limits.rankObservedOnly: Mean position uses actual numbered answer lists only, not prose order.
limits.perplexityWordingUncalibrated: Perplexity wording has not inherited ChatGPT calibration; actual search and citation availability are reported per response.

items.q: Why ask the same question several times?
items.a: Because one answer is not a measurement. Asked four times, the same question produced four completely different citation lists and zero overlap. A run that asked once would report a coin toss as a finding, which is why every number here carries the sample count it came from.

items.q: Why do some questions have no citation rate?
items.a: The model decides whether to search. Wording measured to make it search carries a citation rate; wording a buyer would actually type usually gets answered from memory, and a citation rate over answers that never looked anything up would be a number about nothing.

items.q: It says I was not mentioned. What do I fix?
items.a: The current report can offer evidence-conditioned content, page-citability, third-party-placement or comparison actions when independent reads support them. A content gap applies only to the audited inventory. Missing or incomplete evidence remains unattributed. Historical v1 reports contain observations only.

geo.metaDescription: Ask a real AI assistant your buyers' questions and see which sources it cited, with every denominator shown and no visibility score.
geo.title: See whether AI answers cite your site
geo.subtitle: Eight buyer questions against real ChatGPT answers: five retrieval probes asked three times each, three natural buyer questions asked once. You confirm every fact and every question before anything runs, and the report keeps the retrieval numbers and the natural-demand numbers apart.
geo.accountBoundaryBody: A verified Supabase session is required to run. Each run makes 18 billed provider calls, so it is not available anonymously.
geo.dataBoundaryBody: The report is returned to this page and never written down: no account history, no server copy of the assistant's answer. Minimal billing and quota metadata is kept by the existing credits system. Leaving the page ends the report, so copy anything you need before you go.
geo.howTitle: From buyer questions to observed citations
geo.howBody: Every number in the report is recomputed from the samples underneath it, and a sample that observed nothing is reported as exactly that rather than counted as a zero.
geo.step1Body: Tell the Agent what the site sells, who buys it and which market to ask in. Brand names and the category are proposals until you tick them; nothing is inferred on your behalf.
geo.step2Body: Eight questions are generated from calibrated wording. Edit anything that does not sound like your buyer — an edited retrieval probe is visibly demoted, because its citation counts only meant something for the exact string that was measured.
geo.step3Body: Retrieval probes are asked three times, because one sample cannot tell a site that is not cited apart from a run that happened not to cite it. Natural buyer questions are asked once: repeating a question the assistant answers from memory mostly repeats the same non-observation.
geo.step4Body: Retrieval and natural demand never share a number, prompted and unprompted mentions never share a number, and a probe that failed to trigger a search is excluded as an instrumentation failure rather than counted against you. Copy what you need before you leave — the report is not saved.
geo.finalBoundary: This report observes what one assistant answered at one moment. It is not a ranking, not a forecast, and not a measure of traffic.

limitations.title: What this cannot tell you
limitations.sampling: Samples of one moment. Asking again can return different sources: in calibration, four samples of one question cited 25 hosts between them and not one host appeared in all four.
limitations.platform: A citation is a citation, not a recommendation, a ranking or a traffic estimate.
limitations.citation: A cited page is a page the answer linked to. It is not proof that the page was read, retrieved internally, or found persuasive.
limitations.denominator: Unavailable is not zero. A failed call, an unreadable annotation list and a probe that never searched are excluded rather than counted against you.

recommendations.stage3Body: Ordered by result severity, then by whether this run collected evidence, then by which Agent owns the check, then by observed reach. The confirmed Profile is not part of this ordering. Checks this run could not evaluate are reported separately and never enter the ranking.

seo.recommendation: SEO Agent decision: align search intent first, then adjust the page-specific title, description, headings, internal links, and applicable schema only where captured evidence supports the change.
seo.applicableContext: Use the confirmed target query, page type, country, locale, ICP, and desired outcome to judge whether the proposed search-facing change fits this page.
seo.validation1: Fetch the changed public response and compare it with the captured issue evidence.
seo.validation2: Verify the title, description, headings, links, or schema against visible content and the intended page role.
seo.validation3: Rerun the same bounded checks; use an authorized search source separately when a result depends on search-performance data.
seo.impactSurface: Search intent clarity, snippet inputs, document hierarchy, internal discovery, and structured-data consistency on the affected pages.
seo.risks: A generic rewrite can dilute the page's actual purpose, duplicate another page, or introduce markup that visible content does not support.
seo.limits: This preview does not infer search demand or ranking impact. It cannot replace SERP, traffic, or authorized search-performance evidence.

searchOpportunity.recommendation: Decide whether the confirmed query is worth pursuing before touching the page. Bind country, locale, device, and page, read a SERP snapshot or an authorized Search Console source, then record pursue, refine, or defer together with the evidence behind it.
searchOpportunity.validation1: Re-read the SERP for the same query, country, locale, and device, and note what changed since this run.
searchOpportunity.validation2: Check the recorded decision against the page's actual role: an opportunity no page on the site can answer is a content decision, not a fix.
searchOpportunity.validation3: Before acting on any search-performance number, confirm the authorized source is connected; this run does not read it.
searchOpportunity.impactSurface: Which queries this page competes for, and whether this page is the right place to answer them at all.
searchOpportunity.risks: Pursuing a query on the wrong page splits intent across two pages and leaves both weaker than one clear answer would have been.
searchOpportunity.limits: This preview reads the shape of a result page, not demand. It does not estimate volume, clicks, or position, and it cannot tell you the outcome of pursuing the query.

searchPresentation.recommendation: Rewrite the title and meta description so each states what this page decides for the reader, and so no other page on the site makes the same promise. Keep the wording true to what the page actually contains.
searchPresentation.validation1: Fetch the changed public HTML and confirm the new title and description are what the server returns, not only what the CMS shows.
searchPresentation.validation2: Compare the new text with the sibling pages that shared the old wording and confirm each page now reads differently.
searchPresentation.validation3: Read the first screen of the page and confirm it delivers the promise the snippet just made.
searchPresentation.impactSurface: The title, description, and opening lines a search result is built from, plus how this page reads next to its siblings.
searchPresentation.risks: A rewrite tuned to a query rather than to the page can promise something the page does not deliver, which costs more than the duplicate wording did.
searchPresentation.limits: The character counts here are a reviewed working range, not a rule: results truncate by rendered width. This preview cannot tell you how the snippet will finally be displayed.

contentBrief.recommendation: Treat this as a content brief, not a word-count target. List the decisions a reader still cannot make on this page, write the sections that answer them, and cite where each new claim comes from.
contentBrief.validation1: Re-read the page as the confirmed ICP and check whether the added sections remove a real blocker for them.
contentBrief.validation2: Confirm every added claim has a source that survives review, and delete any sentence that exists only to add length.
contentBrief.validation3: Rerun the same bounded content check and compare it with the measured value captured here.
contentBrief.impactSurface: What the page actually explains, and whether a reader can finish their decision without leaving it.
contentBrief.risks: Padding a page to hit a length target dilutes the parts that already worked, and text lifted from competitors can duplicate a page you already own.
contentBrief.limits: Word count and keyword density are internal heuristics, not documented ranking signals. This preview does not judge content quality and does not predict how the page will perform.

headingStructure.recommendation: Give the page one H1 that names its single decision, use H2s for the steps a reader takes, and H3s for the subquestions each step raises. Fix the outline before changing the wording.
headingStructure.validation1: Fetch the changed page and read only its heading text top to bottom; the outline alone should explain the page.
headingStructure.validation2: Confirm no heading level is skipped and that no heading is used purely for its visual size.
headingStructure.validation3: Check that each H3 section answers its own heading instead of restating it.
headingStructure.impactSurface: The reading order of the page and the structure assistive technology and parsers navigate.
headingStructure.risks: Reshaping headings can break in-page anchors, table-of-contents links, and any styling that keys off heading level.
headingStructure.limits: The H2/H3 counts are a page-type preset and never a blocker. A page with a different but coherent structure can be entirely correct.

internalLinkExposure.recommendation: Give this page a discovery path from a page that is genuinely about the same topic. Pick the source page for its context, write the anchor the way a reader would describe the destination, and add one good link rather than many weak ones.
internalLinkExposure.validation1: Fetch the source page's public HTML and confirm the link sits in the main content, not only inside a template block.
internalLinkExposure.validation2: Follow the link and confirm the destination returns 200 and is the canonical version of the page.
internalLinkExposure.validation3: Rerun the bounded crawl and compare the observed inbound link count with the value captured here.
internalLinkExposure.impactSurface: How a reader and a crawler reach this page from the rest of the site.
internalLinkExposure.risks: Links added for coverage rather than for context read as filler, and repeating one anchor across many pages makes every one of them less descriptive.
internalLinkExposure.limits: This count comes from a bounded same-origin crawl. Navigation the crawl did not reach, and links rendered only by client-side script, are not represented here.

structuredData.recommendation: Mark up only what a reader can already see on the page, and pick the type that matches what the page actually is. When the two disagree, fix the visible content first.
structuredData.validation1: Validate the emitted JSON-LD with a schema validator and confirm every required property is present.
structuredData.validation2: Compare each marked-up value against the rendered page and remove anything the page does not actually show.
structuredData.validation3: Refetch the public HTML and confirm the block is served in the response rather than injected after load.
structuredData.impactSurface: The machine-readable description of this page and its agreement with what the page displays.
structuredData.risks: Markup describing content the page does not show is a policy violation, not a shortcut, and it puts the page's existing eligibility at risk.
structuredData.limits: Valid markup does not entitle a page to a rich result. This preview checks structure and agreement with visible content only, and promises no search feature.

mediaAssets.recommendation: Write alt text that says what each image shows for someone who cannot see it, and treat file format and size as a delivery decision separate from the alt text.
mediaAssets.validation1: Read the page with images disabled and confirm the alt text still carries the meaning.
mediaAssets.validation2: Confirm decorative images carry an empty alt attribute instead of a description.
mediaAssets.validation3: Refetch the page and compare image count, format, and byte size with the values captured here.
mediaAssets.impactSurface: What the page communicates when images do not load or cannot be seen, and how much the page weighs.
mediaAssets.risks: Alt text written for a query instead of for the image misdescribes the page to the readers who depend on it most.
mediaAssets.limits: This is an accessibility and delivery observation. The format and size thresholds here are internal judgment, and no search outcome is implied.

technicalIssueBrief.recommendation: This is a technical condition surfaced during a search review, so write it up instead of fixing it here. Record the observed condition and the search decision it constrains, then hand it to whoever owns the template, CMS, or platform.
technicalIssueBrief.validation1: Confirm the condition still reproduces on the public URL before handing it over.
technicalIssueBrief.validation2: Review the same check in the technical focus, where the owning system and its evidence are in scope.
technicalIssueBrief.validation3: After the owner releases a change, refetch the URL and compare it with the evidence recorded here.
technicalIssueBrief.impactSurface: The search decision this condition constrains; the code or configuration behind it sits outside this Agent.
technicalIssueBrief.risks: Working around a delivery problem in content hides it instead of fixing it, and the workaround usually outlives the person who added it.
technicalIssueBrief.limits: Framework, repository, and owner context are absent here by design. No code or configuration change is prepared, reviewed, or released from this view.

tech.recommendation: Technical fix review: trace the smallest relevant code or configuration surface, confirm the owner and framework, then prepare a change that can be verified against the same evidence.
tech.applicableContext: Confirm the framework, routing layer, hosting behavior, repository owner, release path, and affected templates before translating evidence into code or configuration.
tech.validation1: Reproduce the observed request, response, redirect, directive, or link condition in the owning environment.
tech.validation2: Review the minimal code or configuration diff with the responsible owner and test the affected paths plus a nearby control path.
tech.validation3: After an owner-managed release, fetch the public URL and rerun the same bounded technical checks to compare evidence.
tech.impactSurface: HTTP delivery, crawl paths, index directives, canonical behavior, internal-link integrity, and the specific template or configuration surface involved.
tech.risks: A change without framework and owner context can break routing, deliberate exclusions, localization, caching, or adjacent templates.
tech.limits: Owner and framework context are required before implementation. No site edit, apply, pull request, approval, publish, or deploy occurs here.

indexability.recommendation: Confirm the owner actually intends this URL to be indexable before changing anything: some exclusions are deliberate. Then correct the single status or directive that keeps it out and leave the rest alone.
indexability.validation1: Request the URL exactly as a crawler does, with no cookies or session, and read the final status and headers.
indexability.validation2: Check the same directive on one nearby URL that is deliberately excluded, to confirm the change did not widen.
indexability.validation3: After release, refetch the public URL and rerun this check; use an authorized search source separately to see how the crawler treats it.
indexability.impactSurface: Whether this URL is eligible to be crawled and indexed at all, and every URL that shares the same directive source.
indexability.risks: Directives are usually emitted by shared middleware or a layout, so one edit can silently expose staging paths, filtered views, or thin duplicates.
indexability.limits: This run reads the static response only. Directives added by client-side script, and the crawler's actual indexing decision, are not observed here.

crawl.recommendation: Change robots.txt only where a rule blocks something the owner meant to keep public. Allow the specific path instead of loosening a broad rule, and keep deliberate exclusions in place.
crawl.validation1: Test the exact URL against the new robots.txt with a robots tester before release.
crawl.validation2: Re-test one path that must stay disallowed and confirm it is still blocked.
crawl.validation3: After release, fetch /robots.txt from the public origin and confirm the served file is the one that was reviewed.
crawl.impactSurface: Which paths a crawler is permitted to request, across every URL the affected rule matches.
crawl.risks: robots.txt is prefix-matched and evaluated per user-agent, so a rule written for one path routinely matches more than intended, and disallow does not remove anything already indexed.
crawl.limits: A crawl policy is a request, not an access control. This preview says nothing about authentication, and blocking a URL is not a way to keep it private.

redirect.recommendation: Collapse the chain into a single hop that lands on a 200 HTTPS URL, and point every source at the final destination instead of at the next hop. Use a permanent redirect only when the move is permanent.
redirect.validation1: Request the original URL without following redirects and read each hop's status and Location header in order.
redirect.validation2: Confirm the destination is the canonical URL of the content and returns 200, not another redirect or a soft 404.
redirect.validation3: Test one URL that must not redirect, then refetch after release and compare the hop count with the value captured here.
redirect.impactSurface: The response path for this URL and for every source that links to it, including external links you do not control.
redirect.risks: Redirect rules are ordered and pattern-based, so a new rule can shadow an existing one or create a loop; permanent redirects are cached by browsers and are hard to take back.
redirect.limits: This run follows the public response chain only. Which hop a crawler ultimately honors, and how long a cached permanent redirect persists, are not observed here.

canonical.recommendation: Emit one self-referencing canonical from the page template, using the same absolute URL the server actually serves. Point it elsewhere only when this page is genuinely a duplicate of that target.
canonical.validation1: Fetch the page and confirm exactly one canonical element is present in the served HTML.
canonical.validation2: Confirm the canonical URL returns 200 on its own and matches the served URL character for character, including scheme, host, and trailing slash.
canonical.validation3: Check one paginated, filtered, or parameterized variant of the page and confirm it now consolidates as intended.
canonical.impactSurface: Which URL of this content is treated as the one to keep, and every variant that consolidates into it.
canonical.risks: A canonical pointing at the wrong page asks for this page to be dropped in favor of that one, and a template-wide canonical that hardcodes a single URL does that to every page at once.
canonical.limits: A canonical is a hint, not an instruction, and this run does not fetch the canonical target's status. Consolidation is decided by the search engine, not by this markup.

performance.recommendation: Separate field data from lab data before changing anything: field data says whether real users are affected, lab data says where the time goes. Locate the bottleneck in the owning route or template first, then make one measurable change.
performance.validation1: Read the CrUX p75 over the 28-day window for the same URL and form factor, and remember the window lags any change you ship.
performance.validation2: Run a lab test on the same route before and after the change with identical throttling settings, and compare the specific metric.
performance.validation3: Check one other page on the same template to confirm the change helped there too, not only on the tested URL.
performance.impactSurface: Loading and interaction behavior for this route and every page rendered from the same template or bundle.
performance.risks: Optimizing against a lab number no real user experiences wastes the effort, and deferring or removing resources to move a metric can break functionality that tests do not cover.
performance.limits: Field and lab performance sources are not integrated in this run. Where no measured value is shown above, the threshold comes from the check catalog and not from a measurement of this page.

rendering.recommendation: Compare the static response with the rendered DOM before writing any fix: the difference is exactly what depends on script. Then decide with the framework owner whether the missing content should be server-rendered.
rendering.validation1: Fetch the URL with scripts disabled and list what content is missing from the response.
rendering.validation2: Load the same URL in a browser, compare the rendered DOM with that response, and note which resources blocked rendering.
rendering.validation3: Re-run the comparison after the change and confirm the previously missing content is in the served response.
rendering.impactSurface: What is present in the HTML a crawler receives, versus what appears only after script runs.
rendering.risks: Moving rendering to the server changes caching, personalization, and hydration behavior at once, and a partial move can produce a mismatch that only fails at runtime.
rendering.limits: This run reads the static response only and never executes page script. It cannot tell you whether a crawler rendered the page, or when.

template.recommendation: This value is emitted by a shared template, so fix it once at the source instead of page by page. Derive it from the page's own canonical data, emit it exactly once, and check the routes that share the template.
template.validation1: Identify every route rendered by the same template and pick the two that differ most from each other.
template.validation2: Render both routes and confirm the value is present, distinct, and derived rather than hardcoded.
template.validation3: After release, refetch one page of each type and compare with the evidence captured here.
template.impactSurface: Every page rendered from this template, including routes this bounded crawl never reached.
template.risks: A template fix lands everywhere at once, so a value that is right for one page type can be wrong for another, and a fallback string repeated across routes recreates the duplicate it was meant to remove.
template.limits: This run observed only the pages the bounded crawl reached. Which template owns the value, and how many routes it covers, must be confirmed in the repository.

schema.recommendation: Emit the JSON-LD from the template using the page's own data, and mark up only values the page already displays. Choose the type from what the page is, not from the result you want.
schema.validation1: Validate the emitted block with a schema validator and confirm no required property is missing.
schema.validation2: Compare each property against the rendered page and remove anything the page does not display.
schema.validation3: Check one other page of the same type and confirm the template produced correct, page-specific values there too.
schema.impactSurface: The machine-readable description emitted for every page of this type.
schema.risks: Because the block is generated, one wrong field is wrong on every page of the type, and markup describing content the page does not show is a policy violation.
schema.limits: Valid markup does not entitle a page to any search feature. This run checks presence and parseability only; it does not verify that each value matches the rendered page.

linkIntegrity.recommendation: Take each broken target one at a time and decide whether to repoint it at the live URL, restore the missing page, or remove the link. Fix it where the link is authored, in the template or the content, rather than adding a redirect for every case.
linkIntegrity.validation1: Request each observed target directly and record its final status; a target the crawl could not reach is not automatically broken.
linkIntegrity.validation2: Confirm the corrected link resolves in one hop to a 200 URL, and check one nearby link on the same page as a control.
linkIntegrity.validation3: Rerun the bounded crawl and compare the broken-target count with the value captured here.
linkIntegrity.impactSurface: Whether readers and crawlers can follow this page's outbound links, and every page rendered from the same link source.
linkIntegrity.risks: Deleting a link removes a discovery path other pages may depend on, and redirecting every broken target to the homepage turns a 404 into a soft 404 that is harder to find later.
linkIntegrity.limits: This run classifies only the link targets the bounded crawl collected. Targets it could not reach, and links rendered by client-side script, are not represented here.

internalLinkExposure.recommendation: Give the page a real discovery path: add a contextual internal link from a page that already covers the topic, using anchor text a reader would recognise.
internalLinkExposure.validation1: Confirm the destination is the canonical URL you want indexed, not a redirect or a variant.
internalLinkExposure.validation2: Place the link inside body content a reader actually passes, not in a footer dump.
internalLinkExposure.validation3: Recrawl and compare observed inbound links and click depth for the same page.
internalLinkExposure.impactSurface: Affects whether crawlers and readers can reach the page at all, and how deep it sits from the entry point.
internalLinkExposure.risks: Bulk-adding links to hit a number creates link blocks nobody reads. Add links where the topic genuinely connects.
internalLinkExposure.limits: Inbound links and depth are counted from this bounded crawl only. Links behind JavaScript, pagination, or pages outside the crawl are not observed, and reachability is not a ranking claim.

metadata.impact: Missing or repeated metadata can make page purpose less distinct to readers and search systems. This run does not measure rankings or clicks.
metadata.recommendation: Review the affected pages and give each indexable page metadata that accurately distinguishes its content and intent.
metadata.implementation:
HTML head
  title: [descriptive page title]
  meta description: [page-specific summary]
metadata.validation: Fetch the changed pages, confirm one non-empty intended value per page, then rerun the same bounded check. Validate important templates separately before release.

structure.impact: An unclear heading hierarchy can make the document's main topic and sections harder to understand. The crawl does not measure user behavior.
structure.recommendation: Align the visible heading structure with the page's actual subject, using a clear main heading and descriptive subsections.
structure.implementation:
main
  h1: [one clear page subject]
  section
    h2: [descriptive section]
structure.validation: Inspect the rendered document outline and fetched static HTML, confirm the intended headings are present, then rerun the affected check.

structured_data.impact: Malformed JSON-LD can prevent a parser from understanding the declared entity data. Eligibility for search features is not guaranteed.
structured_data.recommendation: Correct the affected JSON-LD as valid JSON and keep every property consistent with visible page content and the applicable vocabulary.
structured_data.validation: Parse the final static response as JSON, validate the chosen schema type and visible-content consistency, then rerun the check.

crawl.impact: Unexpected response or redirect conditions can reduce how reliably a public URL is fetched. The run does not model every crawler or network.
crawl.recommendation: Trace each affected request, remove unintended hops or failures, and keep one deliberate public destination for the URL.
crawl.implementation:
[requested URL]
  -> [single intended HTTPS destination]
  -> HTTP 2xx static HTML
